# The event loop stays free {#sec-runtime}

Qt delivers input, timers, and queued work through an event loop. If the main thread waits,
the app stops reacting. This one idea explains most Qt rules.

## The event loop {#sec-event-loop}

`QGuiApplication::exec()` starts the main event loop. It waits for input, timer, and other
events, delivers them to their objects, and gives the application a chance to update the next
frame. Each handler must return before the loop can deliver the next event on that thread.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    W[Wait] --> E[Receive event] --> H[Run handler]
    H --> U[Update state and bindings] --> R[Prepare next frame] --> W
```

A long computation in a handler blocks input and prevents the interface from responding. A
timer or asynchronous result lets the handler return; CPU-heavy or blocking work belongs on
another thread. Even repeated short updates can cause a stall if each one starts expensive work.

## Properties drive the view {#sec-properties}

A `Q_PROPERTY` plus a notify signal is observable state. QML binds to it and updates after
the signal. Sketchbook exposes canvas state this way, which leaves QML declarative.

For example, `CanvasStore` declares `snapShapes` with `READ snapShapes`, `WRITE setSnapShapes`,
and `NOTIFY snapShapesChanged`. QML can read or change the property and observe changes. The
setter shows how the contract works:

::: {.snippet source="src/canvas/CanvasStore.cpp"}

```cpp
void CanvasStore::setSnapShapes(bool snap)
    Q_EMIT snapShapesChanged();\n}
```

:::

- The equality check returns when the value has not changed, avoiding unnecessary updates.
- `m_snapShapes = snap` updates the state the getter returns.
- `Q_EMIT snapShapesChanged()` tells Qt to re-evaluate bindings that read the property.

The canvas switch binds its checked state to `root.store.snapShapes` and writes back through
the property when toggled. The declaration in `CanvasStore.hpp` connects that QML property to
this getter, setter, and signal. `CONSTANT` describes a property that never changes; `FINAL`
tells the type system a subclass will not override it.

## Signals cross boundaries {#sec-signals}

A signal announces a change without knowing its listeners. Use typed connections. Give lambdas
a context object so Qt disconnects them when that object dies.

With the default connection, a receiver in the emitting thread runs immediately. A receiver
in another thread receives a queued event, which its event loop handles later. A queued
connection needs a running event loop in the receiver's thread.

Qt's meta-object compiler, `moc`, generates the machinery for classes marked `Q_OBJECT`.
It gives signals, properties, and invokable methods the metadata Qt and QML use. The template
spells the keywords `Q_SIGNALS`, `Q_SLOTS`, and `Q_EMIT` because it disables Qt's short keyword
macros to avoid clashes with other libraries.

## Ownership has one answer {#sec-ownership}

A parent owns its child. A value owns itself. A `std::unique_ptr` owns its pointee. Pick one.
A parented QObject in a `unique_ptr` has two owners and can be deleted twice.

For a QObject with a parent, destroying the parent destroys its children. An unparented object
can instead live on the stack, as a member, or under an owning pointer. The important question
is who destroys it and whether any view or connection can outlive that owner.

## Work leaves the UI thread {#sec-threads}

File operations can block the event loop. Choose the mechanism by the work's shape: use
`QtConcurrent` for an independent task with a result, and a worker object on a `QThread` when
operations need one long-lived, ordered event loop.

### One-shot work: QtConcurrent

`QtConcurrent::run()` is a good fit for an independent operation with a finite input and
result. Copy the input into the task, return a value, then handle it through a context-bound
continuation:

The continuation runs in the context object's thread and is canceled if that object is
destroyed. The task itself does not access the object. Destroying a future does not cancel its
running work, and `QtConcurrent::run()` futures cannot be canceled.

### Ordered I/O: QObject on QThread

Sketchbook has related stateful operations: list, load, save, rename, duplicate, and remove
must share recovery state and execute in submission order. `SketchStorage` remains a GUI-thread
facade. It moves a separate worker to one thread and sends commands with queued invocations:

::: {.snippet source="src/sketchbook/SketchStorage.cpp"}

```cpp
SketchStorage::SketchStorage(QString directory, QObject *parent)
m_thread.start();\n}
```

:::

The `QThread` object stays in the facade's thread; only the worker changes affinity. A queued
invocation runs in the worker's thread, so the GUI never calls worker methods directly. The
facade passes command data by value, and the worker posts results back to the facade through
queued context-bound invocations.

::: {.snippet source="src/sketchbook/SketchStorage.cpp"}

```cpp
void SketchStorage::save(const QString &id, SketchDocument document)
worker->save(id, revision, std::move(document));\n        },\n        Qt::QueuedConnection);\n}
```

:::

On destruction, the facade queues a stop command after accepted work and joins the thread. The
worker quits its own event loop when it reaches that marker. The `finished` connection schedules
worker deletion in its affinity thread:

::: {.snippet source="src/sketchbook/SketchStorage.cpp"}

```cpp
SketchStorage::~SketchStorage()
m_thread.wait();\n}
```

:::

::: {.callout-important}
## QObject affinity is real

Only touch a QObject from its owning thread. Move expensive work away from the UI before it
can block input or trigger repeated expensive updates. Return plain values through a queued
signal or a continuation with a GUI-thread context.
:::
